candidates.teaser: That smell after rain? Scientists discovered it has a name — and a surprisingly dark origin.
candidates.video_title: The Real Reason Rain Has a Smell
candidates.video_description: That iconic post-rain scent has a name: petrichor. It was only identified by scientists in 1964, and its origin involves bacteria releasing spores into the air. What you're actually smelling might surprise you.
candidates.script: That smell after rain isn't water — it's bacteria. Tiny microbes called actinomycetes live in dry soil and release spores the moment raindrops hit the ground. Those spores launch into the air, and your nose is incredibly sensitive to them — detecting concentrations as low as 5 parts per trillion. Scientists didn't even discover this until 1964. So every time you breathe in that 'fresh rain' smell, you're inhaling ancient bacterial spores. Does that make it better or worse?

candidates.teaser: A Mexican island appeared on official maps for 400 years — until the government went to find it and it simply wasn't there.
candidates.video_title: The Island That Vanished From Every Map
candidates.video_description: Bermeja appeared on maps of the Gulf of Mexico from the 1500s all the way to the late 20th century. When Mexican officials sent a search expedition in 2009, the island was completely gone — no geological trace. No one has ever explained it.
candidates.script: An island appeared on official maps for over 400 years — then vanished without a trace. Bermeja was charted in the Gulf of Mexico as far back as 1535. Ships navigated by it. Governments claimed it. In 2009, Mexico sent a full naval expedition to locate it — because owning it meant rights to billions of dollars in oil reserves. They found nothing. No island, no ruins, no seafloor evidence it ever existed. Some maps lied for centuries. But which ones — and why?

candidates.topic: Mirror Test — Animals That Recognize Themselves
candidates.teaser: Most animals completely fail the mirror test — but one creature scientists never expected passed it.
candidates.video_title: The Animal That Knows Its Own Face
candidates.video_description: The mirror self-recognition test is one of the most important benchmarks in animal cognition. Only a handful of species pass it — and one of the most surprising entries on that list is a fish. The cleaner wrasse became the first fish ever recorded to recognize itself in a mirror.
candidates.script: Most animals attack their own reflection thinking it's a rival. Humans figure out mirrors around 18 months old. Only a tiny handful of species have ever passed the mirror self-recognition test — great apes, dolphins, elephants. Then in 2018, scientists tested a tiny reef fish called the cleaner wrasse. It passed. A fish with a brain the size of a grain of rice recognized its own face. Now scientists aren't sure if the test even measures what we thought it did.

candidates.teaser: One sound bounced inside a single room for so long that scientists couldn't believe their instruments were working correctly.
candidates.video_title: This Echo Lasted Over a Minute
candidates.video_description: In a disused oil storage chamber in Scotland, researchers recorded an echo that reverberated for 112 seconds — nearly two full minutes. The Hamilton Mausoleum previously held the world record at 15 seconds. The oil tank shattered every known benchmark for acoustic reverberation.
candidates.script: Someone clapped inside an empty oil tank in Scotland — and the echo didn't stop for 112 seconds. Nearly two full minutes of sound bouncing off concrete walls with nowhere to escape. The previous world record for reverberation was 15 seconds, held by a mausoleum. Scientists had to replay the recording multiple times because they thought the equipment had malfunctioned. The tank is now used as a concert venue. Imagine hearing a single piano note still ringing almost two minutes later.

candidates.topic: Fingernails Grow Faster on Dominant Hand
candidates.teaser: Your fingernails know which hand you use more — and scientists think they know exactly why.
candidates.video_title: Why Your Nails Know You're Right-Handed
candidates.video_description: Fingernails on your dominant hand grow measurably faster than those on your non-dominant hand. They also grow faster in summer, during the day, and on your middle finger specifically. The mechanism behind this reveals something unexpected about how your body distributes resources.
candidates.script: Your fingernails grow faster on whichever hand you use more — and your body has been quietly doing this your entire life. Scientists confirmed it in the 1930s: dominant hand nails grow roughly 0.1 millimeters per day faster. The leading explanation is blood flow. More movement means more circulation, which delivers more keratin to growing cells. Your middle finger also grows fastest of all — and nails grow nearly twice as fast during summer. Your body is constantly measuring how much you use each finger.
